items.title: Bad Bunny Wins Emmy for Super Bowl Halftime Show
items.summary:
Bad Bunny has won his first Emmy, taking outstanding variety special (live) for the Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show. The award caps a strong night for the production, which entered the ceremony with seven nominations.

The halftime show converted nearly all of them, winning in music direction, choreography, sound mixing, lighting design, technical direction and camerawork, and directing alongside the top variety special prize. Jay-Z, an executive producer on the show, picked up his third Emmy as part of the win.

The performance itself was among the most elaborate the Super Bowl has staged, with guest appearances from Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin, a real wedding staged within the set, and actual small business owners incorporated into the production, including the Los Angeles taqueria Villa's Tacos.

Creative director Harriet Cuddeford had described the guiding idea behind the show to Variety, which reported the wins. "The performance is celebrating normal people, and what it is to be human and love and have joy, and really appreciate one another," she said. "This was to show how much he values his community, to celebrate normal people on the world's biggest stage, especially people who are of importance in Latino culture. He's a very authentic person, Benito, and it's about just being authentic and very real and very human."

The haul makes the halftime show one of the ceremony's most decorated single productions and gives Bad Bunny a television award to sit alongside his music career.

items.title: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Lee Chang -dong’s South Korean International Oscar Entry Is Powerful Story Of Class And Desire – Venice Film Festival
items.summary:
Lee Chang-dong's "Possible Love" premiered in competition at the Venice Film Festival, marking the South Korean director's first feature in eight years and arriving as his country's official entry for the International Feature Oscar. The film follows Mi-Ok (Jeon Do-Yeon), a factory worker making masks, and her husband Ho-Seok (Sul Kyung-gu), laid off during a two-year strike and quietly carrying the shame of it.

The story turns when the couple meets Ye-Ti (Cho Yeo-Jeung), a documentarian filming the striking workers, who invites the family to the lavish seaside home she shares with her wealthy husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). Ho-Seok eventually sits for her camera, while Mi-Ok finds herself drawn to Sang-woo, in an encounter in the ocean that plays out with quiet intensity.

Lee traces the film's origins to around 2009, when a mass layoff at a major South Korean company and the suppression of the resulting strike shook the country. He shelved the idea then because the reality resisted fictional treatment, and only found his way in through filmmaking itself as a device within the story.

In its review from Venice, Deadline compared the class divide at the film's center to Bong Joon Ho's "Parasite" while arguing that the pandemic years give Lee's version a different weight, and noted that at nearly three hours the picture takes longer than it needs to find its shape. Once the contrast between the two couples comes into focus, the review said, the film becomes haunting and reaches well past South Korea.

The four leads are given substantial material, and the reviewer suggested viewers unfamiliar with Lee's filmography, which includes "Oasis," "Burning," "Poetry" and "Secret Sunshine," will still find plenty to admire. Producers are Pinehouse Film Co., Ltd., Anonymous Content, LLC and NOWFILM Co., Ltd.

"Possible Love" opens theatrically in the United States on October 23, 2026, followed by a Netflix debut on November 6 after a two-week run in cinemas.

items.title: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’
items.summary:
Wim Wenders used a press conference at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday to revisit the remark that consumed the Berlin Film Festival in February, saying he never told filmmakers to stay out of politics and that the opposite is closer to his position. The German director was in Venice presenting his documentary "From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor."

At the Berlinale, where Wenders served as jury president, he said during the opening press conference that filmmakers are "the counterweight of politics" and must "do the work of people, not the work of politicians." The comments dominated the festival's news cycle, with filmmakers and actors fielding questions about Gaza and ICE raids in the U.S. at their own press conferences, author Arundhati Roy withdrawing in protest, and festival director Tricia Tuttle issuing a statement.

Asked in Venice to reflect, Wenders said the difference is one of mindset rather than engagement. "What I said then was, as filmmakers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that's all I said," he said, adding that filmmakers are "into changing things" while "politics are into confirming what is."

He pushed back directly on how the Berlin remarks traveled. "I hope you're not misquoting me and say we have to stay out of politics, because we do the opposite. We are the antidote," he said, wearing an "Imagine Peace" shirt, according to Variety, which reported the exchange.

The subject had already come up in Venice. At the festival's opening press conference, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said movies are "fundamentally, undeniably political," and framed her answer around the same idea Wenders returned to. "To me, the answer has something to do with empathy," she said. "I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves."

items.title: Wim Wenders on His 14-Year Journey Building Peter Zumthor Doc ‘From Inside Out’
items.summary:
Wim Wenders premiered "From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor" at the Venice Film Festival, closing out a project he began 14 years ago. The two-hour 3D documentary on the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architect is being sold worldwide by HanWay Films, and Brad Pitt, a longtime supporter of Zumthor's work, joined as an executive producer.

The film grew out of a commission. British architect David Chipperfield, curating the 2012 Venice architecture Biennale, asked Wenders for a short on Zumthor, which became a two-day shoot in the architect's small office in Haldenstein, high in the Swiss mountains, and the short "Notes on a Day in the Life of an Architect." "At the end, we shook hands on doing something real together," Wenders told The Hollywood Reporter. "Little did we know that the journey would last 14 years."

The finished documentary ranges across Zumthor's career, from St. Benedict's chapel, completed in 1988, to a memorial for burned witches above the Arctic Circle, to the $724 million David Geffen Galleries at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the architect's largest building and one commissioned nearly two decades ago.

Wenders described his kinship with Zumthor as a shared insistence on changing the work while making it. The architect keeps his office small so he can take only projects he believes in, and refuses to hand a design off once construction begins. "I want to be able to change that script, as I go along. I even want to be able to contradict it," Wenders said of his own process.

On the choice of 3D, Wenders said the format was essential to "Pina," his 2011 film on choreographer Pina Bausch, because that project was fundamentally about space, and that it has not been more necessary since. "From Inside Out" is his tenth 3D work counting shorts and installations.

The film joins a run of artist portraits that includes "Buena Vista Social Club," "Pina," "The Salt of the Earth" and "Anselm," three of which drew Oscar nominations. Asked whether Zumthor's serene buildings amount to a luxury, Wenders offered a limit and a claim: "Buildings cannot repair the world. But they can change our idea of what the world could be."

items.title: Mariska Hargitay Wins Two Emmys For ‘My Mom Jayne,’ Thanks Gloria Steinem From Stage
items.summary:
Mariska Hargitay won two Emmys Saturday night for "My Mom Jayne," the HBO documentary in which she examines the life and career of her mother, actress Jayne Mansfield, and a mystery surrounding her own biological father. The film took Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special, and Hargitay won Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program.

The wins came as the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards opened in Los Angeles with the ceremony formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys. The awards continue Sunday evening from the Peacock Theater and lead into the televised Primetime Emmys on Monday, September 14, on NBC and Peacock, a broadcast Hargitay is hosting.

Onstage, Hargitay invoked Gloria Steinem, who died Wednesday at 92. "My hero and friend Gloria Steinem recently said, 'Please tell your own story,'" she said. "The most important thing we can do for each other is to know each other through stories. I got to know my mother through telling the story. It's a gift that's indescribable." Accepting the directing award, she said it took her time to understand the film was hers to make: "I could direct it."

"My Mom Jayne" beat "John Candy: I Like Me," "Marty, Life Is Short," "Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!" and "Ocean with David Attenborough," which won for cinematography and sound editing. In the directing race, Hargitay was up against Lawrence Kasdan, Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio, Alexandria Stapelton and Rebecca Miller, whose five-part "Mr. Scorsese" won Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Series.

Backstage, Hargitay described a stretch that also included her Broadway debut in "Every Brilliant Thing" and her 28th season starring on "Law & Order: SVU," Deadline reported. "I'm at a place in my life where I just say yes," she said. "It's a year of firsts and a year of saying yes. Not limiting myself or not being governed by fear."
